headline: Gator blues crash the Sound as bass bite goes technical at Execution Rocks
subhead: Big stripers still feeding on mackerel, but you need to work the structure right.
body_markdown:
The Western Sound is in full summer mode now, and if you know how to read the water, you're going to put fish in the boat. But this isn't May anymore — the easy bite is over, and you better have your game tight.

The big news this week is the arrival of serious bluefish. I'm talking gator blues, not cocktails. These fish are pushing 15 pounds and they're absolutely destroying everything in their path. The action is concentrated from Matinecock Point east to the Stepping Stones, where the deeper water holds cooler temps and more oxygen. These blues are feeding on the same mackerel that have been driving the bass bite, and when you find one species, you'll find the other.

Speaking of bass, the oversize fish are still here, but they've gotten selective. The days of throwing anything with hooks and getting crushed are behind us. Water temps are climbing toward 70, and that's pushing the quality fish to specific structure at specific tide stages. Execution Rocks continues to be the money spot, but you need to fish it right. The ledge on the north side holds fish on the outgoing tide — not the flood, not slack, but when that water is moving hard off the shelf. I'm seeing 40-inch fish coming off mojos trolled tight to the structure, but only when the current is ripping.

The mackerel bite is still the key to everything. These baitfish are thick from Hart Island to Oyster Bay, and they're what's keeping the big fish around. If you're trolling, large mojos in bunker patterns are producing. If you're chunking, fresh mackerel strips on a fishfinder rig will get you bit. The umbrella rig bite has been solid too, especially early morning when the fish are up in the water column.

Topwater action is happening, but it's become a timing game. First light and last light are your windows, and you need moving water. The Throgs Neck Bridge pilings have been holding fish on the flood tide — bass are ambushing bait as it gets swept through the structure. Super Strike plugs in bunker patterns are getting crushed, but you've got maybe a 30-minute window before the fish go deep.

Fluke fishing has been steady but not spectacular. The better fish are coming from deeper water — 30 to 40 feet along the channel edges from Little Neck Bay to Manhasset Bay. White Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails are the go-to rig. The key is working the drift slow and keeping contact with bottom. I'm seeing keeper fish to 6 pounds, but you're going to sort through plenty of shorts.

Porgies have moved in strong around the rocky structure. The docks at Oyster Bay and the rocks off Matinecock Point are holding good numbers of fish to 2 pounds. Standard porgy rigs with clam are producing, but you want to fish the top and bottom of the tide when the current slows down.

Weakfish are making a showing in the back bays. Jamaica Bay has been producing keeper fish on the grass shrimp that are flushing out of the creeks. It's not a wide-open bite, but if you're targeting them specifically with light tackle and small baits, you can put a few in the box.

The bait situation tells the whole story. Mackerel schools are everywhere, peanut bunker are starting to show in decent numbers, and the grass shrimp are thick in the back waters. This is classic late June — the spring migration is winding down, but the summer residents are settling in.

Looking ahead, we're approaching the new moon on Friday, which means big tides and strong currents. That's going to fire up the bite at all the structure spots. The bass that have been finicky will start feeding more aggressively when that water really starts moving. I'm watching for the first real weakfish push as these spring tides flush more bait out of the back bays. Water temps are going to keep climbing, so the window for consistent bass action is narrowing, but the blues should only get better as we head into July.
